title: Heap
html:
A heap gives you the smallest (or largest) element of a changing collection in O(1), with O(log n) insert and remove. Almost every “top k”, “k-way merge” and “running statistic” problem is a heap of the right type and the right size.

Binary heap — a complete binary tree stored in an array where every node is <= its children (min-heap) or >= its children (max-heap). The root is therefore the minimum (or maximum). A priority queue is the abstract interface; a binary heap is its usual implementation.

OperationTimeHow
peek() — min or maxO(1)it is a[0]
push(x)O(log n)append, then sift up while smaller than the parent
pop()O(log n)move the last element to the root, then sift down
heapify(array)O(n)sift down from the last internal node to the root — cheaper than n pushes
search for an arbitrary keyO(n)a heap is not sorted; only the root is special
Key point

The heap property says nothing about the order between siblings or between subtrees — a[1..] is not sorted. Printing the array of a heap or iterating a PriorityQueue gives an arbitrary-looking order; to get sorted output you must pop repeatedly.

Priority queues in each language

LanguageTypeDefaultMax-heap
Pythonheapq functions on a listmin-heappush -x, negate on pop (or (-key, item) tuples)
C++std::priority_queue<T>max-heapdefault; min-heap needs priority_queue<T, vector<T>, greater<T>>
Javajava.util.PriorityQueue<T>min-heapnew PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder()) or a comparator
JavaScriptnone built in—write a small Heap class with a comparator once (below) and reuse it
Key point

The JavaScript Heap class above is reused unchanged in every solution below — comparator (a, b) => a - b for a min-heap, (a, b) => b - a for a max-heap, or compare a field of an array/object. Python's heapq compares tuples lexicographically, which is how (key, payload) pairs are ordered in the k-closest and merge problems.

Pitfall

Python: heapq.heappush(h, -x) and forgetting to negate on the way out is the classic max-heap slip. Java: (a, b) -> b - a overflows for values near Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE — use Integer.compare(b, a) or Collections.reverseOrder(). C++: remember the default priority_queue is a max-heap.

Sort a k-sorted (nearly sorted) array

Example

Input: arr = [9, 8, 7, 18, 19, 17], k = 2
Output: 7 8 9 17 18 19
Input: arr = [10, 9, 8, 7, 4, 70, 60, 50], k = 4
Output: 4 7 8 9 10 50 60 70

Every element is at most k positions away from its sorted position. A full sort is O(n log n); exploiting k gives O(n log k).

Idea

The element that belongs at index i lies somewhere in arr[i..i+k]. So keep a min-heap of the next k+1 unplaced elements: its minimum is guaranteed to be the next output. Push one element, and whenever the heap holds k+1 items pop its minimum into the result; drain the heap at the end.

Time O(n log k)Space O(k)
Pitfall

The heap must hold k + 1 elements before you trust its minimum, not k: with k = 2 and [9, 8, 7, …], the 7 is only pushed as the third element. Popping after k pushes would emit 8 first. When k >= n the method degenerates to heap sort — still correct, just O(n log n).

Purchase maximum items with a budget

Example

Input: cost = [1, 12, 5, 111, 200], budget = 10
Output: 2 (buy 1 and 5)
Input: cost = [20, 10, 5, 30, 100], budget = 35
Output: 3 (buy 5, 10 and 20)

Idea

Greedy: always buy the cheapest remaining item — a more expensive one can never let you afford more items. Sorting gives the cheapest items in order in O(n log n):

Time O(n log n)Space O(1) extra (in-place sort)

But you usually stop long before the end — the budget runs out after r items. A min-heap built in O(n) and popped r times costs O(n + r log n), which beats a sort when r is small (a tight budget, a huge catalogue).

Time O(n + r log n)Space O(n)
Key point

The original notes' heap version had two bugs: it iterated for i in cost while popping from the same list (pq = cost aliases, it does not copy), and the driver called the sorting function instead. Copy the list before heapify, and loop on the heap's top, not on an index.

K largest elements

Example

Input: arr = [5, 15, 10, 20, 8], k = 2
Output: 15 20
Input: arr = [3, 9, 1, 7, 5, 8], k = 3
Output: 7 8 9

Idea

Keep a min-heap of size k holding the k largest elements seen so far. Its root is the smallest of those k — the threshold. A new element that is not above the threshold can never be in the answer; one that is replaces the root. The heap is tiny, so each step is O(log k).

1
Build
Put the first k elements into a min-heap.
2
Scan the rest
If x <= heap.top() ignore it; otherwise pop the top and push x.
3
Collect
The heap now holds exactly the k largest. Pop them for ascending order.
Time O(n log k)Space O(k)

The alternative is a max-heap of all n elements, popped k times. It is simpler and gives the results largest-first, but it needs O(n) memory and cannot process a stream:

ApproachTimeSpaceWorks on a stream?
sort, take the last kO(n log n)O(1)no
max-heap of all, pop kO(n + k log n)O(n)no
min-heap of size kO(n log k)O(k)yes — the heap is the running answer
quickselectO(n) averageO(1)no (unordered result)
Pitfall

Use a min-heap for the k largest and a max-heap for the k smallest. The heap type is the opposite of what you are looking for, because the root must be the element you are willing to throw away.

K closest elements to x

Example

Input: arr = [10, 15, 7, 3, 4], x = 8, k = 2
Output: 7 10
Input: arr = [5, 15, 10, 20, 8], x = 12, k = 3
Output: 8 10 15

Pick the k elements with the smallest |arr[i] - x|. The naive approach finds the closest element, removes it and repeats k times:

Time O(n · k)Space O(k)
Idea

This is k smallest with the key |arr[i] - x|, so flip the previous recipe: a max-heap of size k keyed on the distance. The root is the farthest of the current best k; a new element closer than it replaces it. Store (distance, value) pairs so the heap orders by distance but you can still print the value.

Time O(n log k)Space O(k)
Key point

Ties matter: two elements at the same distance (7 and 9 for x = 8) — decide which one wins before coding and encode it in the comparator (here: on equal distance the larger value is dropped, so the smaller one is kept). Python's tuple ordering, C++'s pair ordering and the explicit Java/JavaScript comparators all implement that same rule. If the array is sorted, a two-pointer window or binary search solves it in O(log n + k) with no heap at all.

Merge k sorted arrays

Example

Input: arrays = [[10, 20, 30], [5, 15], [1, 9, 11, 18]]
Output: 1 5 9 10 11 15 18 20 30

N is the total number of elements, k the number of arrays. Two obvious approaches ignore the fact that the inputs are already sorted:

Idea

At any moment the next output is the smallest among the heads of the k arrays. Keep those k heads in a min-heap as (value, array index, element index). Pop the minimum, append it, and push the next element of the same array. Each of the N elements enters and leaves a heap of size <= k once.

Time O(N log k)Space O(k) for the heap, plus the output
ApproachTimeWhy
concatenate + sortO(N log N)throws away the input order
merge one array at a timeO(N · k)the growing result is re-merged k - 1 times
min-heap of k headsO(N log k)every element passes once through a heap of size k
divide and conquer (merge pairs)O(N log k)same bound, no heap, more copying
Pitfall

Push the array index and position, not just the value — otherwise you cannot tell which array to advance. Pushing the whole remaining array into the heap instead of one head makes it O(N log N) again. The same heap-of-heads pattern merges k sorted linked lists, k sorted files on disk (external sorting) and k sorted streams.

Median of a stream

Example

Input: stream = [25, 7, 10, 15, 20]
Output: 25.0 16.0 10.0 12.5 15.0

After each new number, report the median of everything seen so far. A median needs the middle of the data, not its minimum — the trick is to split the data in two halves.

Numbers so farSortedMedian
252525.0
25 77 25(7 + 25) / 2 = 16.0
25 7 107 10 2510.0
25 7 10 157 10 15 25(10 + 15) / 2 = 12.5
25 7 10 15 207 10 15 20 2515.0

Re-sorting after every arrival works but costs O(n log n) per element (or O(n) with insertion into a sorted list):

Time O(n² log n) totalSpace O(n)
Idea

Two heaps. Keep the smaller half in a max-heap small and the larger half in a min-heap large, with |small| - |large| kept at 0 or 1. The median is then small.top() (odd count) or the average of the two tops (even count). Every insertion is two or three heap operations.

1
Push x into small
The max-heap of the lower half.
2
Move small.top() to large
Guarantees every element of small is <= every element of large, even if x was big.
3
Rebalance
If large has more elements than small, move large.top() back. Now |small| = |large| or |small| = |large| + 1.
4
Read the median
small.top() when small is bigger, else (small.top() + large.top()) / 2.
Time O(log n) per elementSpace O(n)
Key point

An augmented BST (each node storing its subtree size, as in the BST topic) also works: insert in O(h), then find the n/2-th and n/2 + 1-th smallest in O(h). It additionally supports deleting elements (a sliding-window median), which the two heaps cannot do cheaply. For a pure stream the two heaps are simpler and faster.

Pitfall

Pushing x straight into whichever heap looks right (x < small.top() → small) and only then rebalancing is also correct, but it has more branches and an empty-heap edge case. The push-then-move routine above has no special cases. And compute the average in floating point (/ 2.0): integer division would print 12 for 12.5.

Choosing the heap

ProblemHeap typeHeap sizeTime
k largest / k-th largestmin-heapkO(n log k)
k smallest / k closestmax-heap (on the key)kO(n log k)
sort a k-sorted arraymin-heapk + 1O(n log k)
merge k sorted arraysmin-heap of headskO(N log k)
buy cheapest first / schedule by prioritymin-heap of everythingnO(n + r log n)
running medianmax-heap + min-heapn/2 eachO(log n) per element
Do

Ask two questions for every heap problem: what key does the heap order by (value, distance, array head) and how large may it grow (k, k + 1, n). The root is always the element you are prepared to discard.

Interview Q&A

Why is building a heap O(n) when n inserts cost O(n log n)?

heapify sifts down from the last internal node to the root. Most nodes are near the bottom and sift only a step or two; summing height × nodes-at-that-height over the tree gives O(n). Pushing one at a time sifts up from the bottom, where most nodes have log n ancestors — O(n log n).

Why a min-heap for the k largest elements?

The heap holds the current best k and its root is the smallest of them — the only one that can be evicted. A new element either fails to beat that root (ignore it) or replaces it. With a max-heap the root is the best element, which you would never want to evict, so you would have to keep all n elements.

Heap or balanced BST for a running median?

Two heaps: O(log n) per element and only the two tops are ever read. A balanced BST augmented with subtree sizes also gives O(log n) and can additionally delete elements (sliding-window median) and answer any order statistic, at the price of a far bigger implementation — Python and JavaScript have no built-in ordered set to lean on.

How do you get a max-heap in Python, and what is the catch?

heapq only implements a min-heap, so push -x and negate when popping; for records push (-key, item) tuples. The catch is forgetting the negation on the way out, and for tuples that ties on the key fall through to comparing the payload — make the payload comparable (an index) or wrap it.

Does a priority queue preserve insertion order for equal priorities?

No — binary heaps are not stable. If FIFO order among equal priorities matters, store a sequence number as a secondary key: (priority, seq, item). The same trick breaks ties deterministically in the k-closest problem.

What are the time bounds of the heap operations and why is search O(n)?

peek is O(1), push and pop are O(log n) (one root-to-leaf path), heapify is O(n). A heap only orders parent against children, so an arbitrary key can be anywhere below the root; finding or deleting it needs a linear scan, or an auxiliary index map (the indexed heap used by Dijkstra's decrease-key).
